content: Mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HIV is the most common way children acquire HIV worldwide. While effective interventions have been developed to prevent HIV transmission during pregnancy and childbirth, a significant proportion of MTCT occurs postnatally through breastfeeding. This systematic review aimed to evaluate interventions designed to reduce late postnatal MTCT of HIV, assess their efficacy in reducing transmission, and determine their impact on overall survival and HIV-free survival. The review included six randomized clinical trials and one intervention cohort study. Two trials investigated the impact of reducing or eliminating breastfeeding. In one trial comparing breastfeeding to formula feeding, formula feeding significantly reduced the risk of HIV transmission (36.7% HIV infection rate at 24 months in the breastfeeding group versus 20.5% in the formula group, p = 0.001). However, mortality and malnutrition rates during the first two years of life were similar between the two groups. Another trial examined early cessation of breastfeeding, finding no significant difference in HIV-free survival between children who stopped breastfeeding abruptly at four months and those who continued breastfeeding. A trial on vitamin supplementation found that children of mothers receiving vitamin A had higher rates of HIV infection, while no efficacy was demonstrated for other vitamin supplements. An intervention cohort study assessed the risk of MTCT by six months of age based on infant feeding practices. It found that breastfed infants who were also given solid foods had a significantly higher risk of HIV transmission (hazard ratio = 10.87, p = 0.018). However, formula-fed infants had a higher cumulative three-month mortality rate compared to exclusively breastfed infants (hazard ratio = 2.06, p = 0.051). Three trials evaluated the use of antiretroviral prophylaxis in breastfeeding infants. In a trial conducted in Botswana, mothers received zidovudine during late pregnancy and labor, and both mothers and infants were randomized to receive either a two-dose nevirapine regimen or placebo. Infants were further randomized to either six months of breastfeeding with zidovudine prophylaxis or formula feeding with one month of zidovudine. The transmission rate was lower in the formula-fed group (5.6%) compared to the breastfeeding group (9.0%, p = 0.04). However, HIV-free survival rates at 18 months were similar between the two groups (p = 0.60). Two trials investigated extended infant nevirapine prophylaxis. In one trial, a six-week course of nevirapine reduced the risk of HIV transmission by six weeks of age (p = 0.009), but not at six months (p = 0.016). In another trial, mothers were advised to exclusively breastfeed for six months and consider weaning thereafter. Infants who received nevirapine until 14 weeks of age (5.2%) or nevirapine with zidovudine until 14 weeks of age (6.4%) had significantly lower risks of HIV transmission by nine months compared to a control group receiving two-dose nevirapine (10.6%, p < 0.001). HIV-free survival was significantly better in both extended prophylaxis groups through nine months and in the extended nevirapine group through 15 months. In conclusion, complete avoidance of breastfeeding effectively prevents MTCT of HIV but is associated with significant risks, such as diarrheal illness if formula is prepared with unclean water. If breastfeeding is practiced, two interventions are effective in reducing HIV transmission: exclusive breastfeeding during the first few months of life and extended antiretroviral prophylaxis for the infant (either nevirapine alone or nevirapine with zidovudine).
